stem:
A 66-year-old retired plumber who has smoked for most of his adult life has had a dry cough for two months and now speaks in a weak, rough voice. Chest X-ray shows a left hilar mass with fullness of the mediastinum beside the aortic arch. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal cord is paralysed and fixed.

Which structure has most likely been involved by the tumour?

options.A: Left phrenic nerve running over the surface of the pericardium
options.B: Right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking round the subclavian artery
options.C: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve looping beneath the aortic arch
options.D: Left stellate ganglion lying at the apex of the left lung
options.E: Left hypoglossal nerve passing through the upper part of the neck

correct_answer: C. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve looping beneath the aortic arch
why_correct: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the vagus and hooks under the aortic arch, so a left hilar or mediastinal tumour (or involved nodes) can compress or invade it. This causes vocal cord palsy with a weak, hoarse voice, and hoarseness in a smoker is a red flag for lung or laryngeal cancer. Persistent hoarseness with a chest X-ray abnormality needs urgent assessment on the suspected cancer pathway. Source: NICE NG12 suspected cancer recognition and referral (2015, updated); standard anatomy teaching.
why_wrong: A. Phrenic nerve involvement causes hemidiaphragm paralysis and breathlessness, not hoarseness. B. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops round the right subclavian artery, so a left-sided hilar mass does not usually reach it and the paralysed cord here is on the left. D. Stellate ganglion involvement gives Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) rather than a voice change. E. The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue and lies in the neck, away from the mediastinum, so it would cause tongue deviation, not hoarseness.
pearl: Because the left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the aortic arch, left-sided mediastinal disease is the classic cause of lung-cancer-related vocal cord palsy.
thinking: Hoarse voice in a smoker with a chest mass  ↓  Vocal cord palsy suggests nerve involvement  ↓  Which nerve loops under the aortic arch on the left?  ↓  Left recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: Choosing the phrenic nerve because it also runs through the mediastinum, forgetting that it affects the diaphragm and not the voice.
takeaway: Hoarseness with a left hilar or mediastinal lung tumour points to left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.
notes: Adapted with a left hilar mass and fixed left cord so the item tests sidedness and anatomy (left RLN under aortic arch). Live PAQ15950 tests RLN palsy from a thyroid mass (different cause and site), so scenario and learning point differ. NICE NG12 and RLN course cited as standard teaching; no web page fetched. PAN4980 (same learning point) skipped to avoid repeating it within this batch.
Same learning point as PAN4512 (RLN involvement by lung tumour causes hoarseness), which is written in this batch; not repeated twice. Also near live PAQ15950 (RLN, thyroid mass).

stem:
A 47-year-old woman attends clinic for follow-up of pulmonary sarcoidosis. She has become very thirsty, passes large volumes of urine and has been constipated for several weeks. Her adjusted calcium is raised, her parathyroid hormone level is suppressed and her chest X-ray shows stable hilar nodes.

Which mechanism best explains her raised calcium?

options.A: Conversion of vitamin D to its active form by macrophages in the granulomas
options.B: Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide by the granulomatous tissue
options.C: Autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone by a parathyroid adenoma
options.D: Osteolytic destruction of bone by metastatic deposits within the skeleton
options.E: Impaired excretion of calcium because of established renal failure

correct_answer: A. Conversion of vitamin D to its active form by macrophages in the granulomas
why_correct: Activated macrophages in sarcoid granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D without normal feedback control. This increases gut calcium absorption and bone resorption, raising calcium while PTH is suppressed. Treatment is usually with oral corticosteroids, and vitamin D supplements and a high calcium intake should be avoided. Source: standard teaching on sarcoidosis (British Thoracic Society sarcoidosis guidance, 2008).
why_wrong: B. PTHrP is secreted by some solid tumours and causes hypercalcaemia of malignancy, not sarcoidosis. C. A parathyroid adenoma would give a raised or inappropriately normal PTH, whereas her PTH is suppressed. D. Bone metastases cause hypercalcaemia in cancer, but nothing here suggests malignancy. E. Renal failure usually lowers calcium (reduced vitamin D activation), and nothing suggests she has kidney failure.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia with a suppressed PTH in granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB) is driven by extrarenal vitamin D activation.
thinking: Sarcoidosis with thirst, polyuria and constipation  ↓  Hypercalcaemia with low PTH means PTH-independent  ↓  Granulomas contain 1-alpha-hydroxylase  ↓  Excess active vitamin D
exam_trap: Selecting PTHrP because it is a well-known cause of PTH-independent hypercalcaemia, when granulomatous disease works through vitamin D.
takeaway: Sarcoid hypercalcaemia arises from macrophage activation of vitamin D, not from PTH or PTHrP.
notes: Vignette changed to clinic follow-up with suppressed PTH added so the key is PTH-independent. Same mechanism kept (extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylase). No live item covers the sarcoid hypercalcaemia mechanism (searched sarcoid, hypercalc, vitamin D). Cited as standard teaching/BTS; no page fetched.

stem:
A 58-year-old man has spent twenty years drilling and sandblasting granite in a quarry, usually without a face mask. He now has progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. His chest X-ray shows many small nodules in the upper zones and thin rim-like calcification around enlarged hilar lymph nodes.

Which inhaled agent is most likely to be responsible?

options.A: Asbestos fibres released from old building insulation materials
options.B: Coal dust inhaled during years of underground mining work
options.C: Raw cotton fibres inhaled in the preparation rooms of textile mills
options.D: Beryllium fumes released during the manufacture of metal alloys
options.E: Crystalline silica dust released from cutting and blasting rock

correct_answer: E. Crystalline silica dust released from cutting and blasting rock
why_correct: Crystalline silica from cutting, drilling or blasting stone, sand and granite causes silicosis, a pneumoconiosis with small upper-zone nodules and hilar nodes that may show eggshell calcification. Risk rises with cumulative dust exposure, and dust control and masks reduce it. People with silicosis also have an increased risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer. Source: standard occupational respiratory teaching; Health and Safety Executive silica guidance.
why_wrong: A. Asbestos causes lower-zone fibrosis, pleural plaques and mesothelioma rather than upper-zone nodules with eggshell calcification. B. Coal dust causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis, which also favours the upper zones, but the exposure here is rock cutting, not mining. C. Cotton fibres cause byssinosis, an asthma-like illness that is worse at the start of the working week. D. Beryllium causes a granulomatous disease resembling sarcoidosis, linked to alloy and electronics industries rather than stone work.
pearl: Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is a classic radiological clue to silicosis, and these patients need to be alert to tuberculosis symptoms.
thinking: Years of sandblasting granite  ↓  Upper-zone nodules and eggshell hilar nodes  ↓  Pneumoconiosis from a mineral dust  ↓  Silica
exam_trap: Choosing asbestos because it is the best-known occupational lung toxin, ignoring the upper-zone nodular pattern.
takeaway: Stone, sand or granite dust exposure with upper-zone nodules and eggshell node calcification means silicosis.
notes: New vignette (quarry sandblaster, eggshell calcification). Live DT120 uses a stonemason with known silicosis but tests the TB work-up (key sputum AFB), so the learning point of identifying silica as the cause is not live. No web page fetched; cited as standard teaching.

stem:
A 72-year-old retired ship pipe-fitter has had over a year of worsening breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. For decades he stripped old lagging from engine-room pipework. He has finger clubbing and fine late-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. His chest X-ray shows lower-zone reticular shadowing with calcified plaques along the pleura.

Which condition best explains his lung disease?

options.A: Silicosis from inhaled quartz dust particles over many years
options.B: Asbestosis, a fibrosing lung disease from asbestos fibres
options.C: Sarcoidosis with chronic pulmonary parenchymal involvement
options.D: Malignant pleural mesothelioma with encasement of the lung
options.E: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis from repeated antigen exposure

correct_answer: B. Asbestosis, a fibrosing lung disease from asbestos fibres
why_correct: Prolonged heavy asbestos exposure causes asbestosis, a diffuse interstitial fibrosis worst at the lung bases, with fine basal crackles, clubbing and pleural plaques on imaging. It typically appears 20 to 40 years after exposure. The fibrosis gives a restrictive pattern with reduced gas transfer. Source: standard occupational respiratory teaching; the occupational history is the key to diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Silicosis causes nodules predominantly in the upper zones after silica dust exposure, not lower-zone fibrosis with pleural plaques. C. Sarcoidosis commonly shows hilar lymphadenopathy and upper-zone change, and neither the pleural calcification nor the occupational history fits. D. Mesothelioma presents with chest pain, effusion and irregular pleural thickening rather than bibasal crackles and reticular change. E. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis follows organic antigen exposure and often causes episodic symptoms with upper or mid-zone change.
pearl: Pleural plaques show past asbestos exposure but do not themselves cause breathlessness, whereas asbestosis does.
thinking: Decades stripping lagging with exertional breathlessness  ↓  Clubbing and bibasal crackles with lower-zone reticulation  ↓  Pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure  ↓  Asbestosis
exam_trap: Choosing mesothelioma because of asbestos, when the picture is fibrosis with crackles rather than pleural pain or effusion.
takeaway: Bibasal crackles, clubbing and lower-zone fibrosis after heavy asbestos exposure indicate asbestosis.
notes: Live PAQ15445 (asymptomatic pleural plaques, key asbestos), RES024 and PAAKT025 (mesothelioma) differ: this tests asbestos-related parenchymal fibrosis. No live asbestosis item found. Standard teaching; no page fetched.

stem:
A 68-year-old man worked underground at a coal mine for thirty-five years. He now gets breathless on exertion, and his chest X-ray shows multiple small rounded opacities in both upper zones. The respiratory doctor explains that his illness belongs to a group of interstitial lung diseases caused by inhaling mineral dusts at work.

What is the collective name for this group of conditions?

options.B: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis from organic antigens
options.C: Chronic obstructive bronchitis from tobacco smoke
options.D: Benign pleural plaque disease after asbestos

correct_answer: E. Pneumoconiosis, the dust-related lung diseases
why_correct: Pneumoconiosis is the collective term for lung diseases caused by inhaling mineral dusts such as coal dust, silica and asbestos. Coal worker's pneumoconiosis typically shows small nodular opacities in the upper zones after prolonged underground exposure. It is a prescribed industrial disease in the UK, so the occupational history can matter for benefits. Source: standard occupational respiratory teaching; UK Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit scheme.
why_wrong: A. Occupational asthma is a variable airway disease caused by workplace sensitisers, not dust-related parenchymal change. B. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis is a hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled organic antigens, not mineral dusts. C. Chronic obstructive bronchitis is airway disease mainly from smoking and does not describe mineral dust fibrosis. D. Pleural plaques are a marker of asbestos exposure and not the name for the whole group.
pearl: The suffix -osis in pneumoconiosis reflects chronic dust-induced fibrosis, and silicosis, asbestosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis all fall within it.
thinking: Long-term coal mine work with upper-zone nodules  ↓  Mineral dust is deposited in the lung  ↓  Chronic fibrotic response  ↓  Pneumoconiosis
exam_trap: Confusing a dust-induced fibrotic disease with occupational asthma, which involves variable airflow limitation instead.
takeaway: Pneumoconiosis is the umbrella term for lung disease caused by inhaling mineral dusts at work.
notes: Rewritten as a coal-miner vignette; the live bank has no item naming pneumoconiosis (searched pneumoconi, silicosis, coal, dust). Key term is not a movable threshold. Standard teaching; no page fetched.
